She felt it when he let go of whatever he’d been holding up. It went out of him in one long breath against her shoulder, and his arms tightened, and he didn’t lift his head.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the bedroom she took his watch off his wrist and put it on the table. She undid his shirt and he stood still and let her, the way he’d let her hold him in the lift in Hong Kong, as if he were learning a language by ear. She folded the shirt over the chair. She asked if he wanted a shower and he shook his head, and she turned back the covers, and he got in and turned towards her at once and pulled her against him until there was no gap anywhere.

“You’re tired,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“No.”

“Okay.”

She’d almost fallen asleep when he spoke into her hair.

“She was young.”

She went still.

“She was in the stairwell. I keep thinking about the last person who saw her. Whether they knew it was the last time. Whether she knew,” he said, low.

Si-Jie put her palm flat on his cheek in the dark.

“You don’t have to know tonight. You can think about it tomorrow,” she said.

“I can’t switch it off. I keep going through the sequence. I need to understand what happened.”

She didn’t tell him to stop caring. She didn’t tell him it didn’t matter. “I know you do. Then let me keep you here for a bit. Just tonight.”

He was quiet. Then his arm came tighter round her.

“I don’t always come back straight away. Sometimes I finish work and I’m still there. I might not be good company,” he said.

“You’re already terrible company. You’re quiet, you hardly talk, and you drink coffee like a punishment.”

She felt him almost laugh against her hair.

“I don’t want you to feel you have to wait for me.”

She tucked herself under his chin. “I don’t feel I have to. I want to. Listen. You don’t have to come home happy. You don’t have to come home ready to talk, or explain everything in your head. But you have to come home. To me.”

He didn’t answer for so long that she thought she’d said too much. Then he pressed his mouth to her hair.

“I’ll try,” said Arthur, and this time when he closed his eyes they stayed closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the other side of the bed was empty, and she found him in the kitchen in a clean shirt making coffee, with two plates on the counter: eggs, toast, fruit, and a glass of water by hers.

She put her arms round his waist from behind. “You made breakfast.”

“For both of us.”

She turned him round by the shirt and looked up at his face. The shadows were still there. But he was looking at her, at her, all the way.

“You’re back,” she said.

He understood what she meant. He bent and kissed her, and stayed there with his forehead on hers.

“I might be late again tonight.”

“I know.”

“I’ll message you. And I’ll eat. Properly.”

“Good boyfriend,” said Si-Jie.

He considered the word. “That one’s acceptable.”

He left at quarter past nine. By the time the lift reached the ground floor she’d sent four messages: eat lunch, drink water, don’t stare at the board for twenty minutes without moving, I’m serious. He answered from the lobby.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Love you.

He stood in the lobby with the phone in his hand and the doors sliding open and shut in front of him. He’d been not saying it for three months. It had seemed, all that time, like the careful thing.

Arthur: Love you too.

He put his phone in his pocket and went out to the car. The case wasn’t finished. The man on the stairs was still out there. But at three in the morning he’d come home to someone who hadn’t needed him to explain the dark before she held him, and he was beginning to understand that she might be the only way he knew how to come back.

chapters.title: Her Thesis
chapters.desc: Her thesis needs participants, and her boyfriend reads the consent form to the end before he signs it. Question nine asks whether he finds it easy to let someone close. He answers without words, and then with a few.
chapters.epigraph: “The forty messages are how I know you’re coming back.”
chapters.content:
Arthur Kao had been questioned by suspects, cross-examined by lawyers and assessed by colleagues who thought his emotional restraint was a professional flaw. He’d never been especially concerned about any of it.

Then Yen Si-Jie came at him with a questionnaire.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her thesis proposal had taken longer to approve than she’d expected. Not because the subject was controversial, but because research on adult attachment meant careful thought about privacy, distress, informed consent and the limits of what anyone could honestly conclude. On the second Tuesday in February the ethics committee finally signed it off, and her supervisor called her in to make one thing clear.

“Your participants mustn’t feel that their answers will affect their relationship with you. That goes double for anyone you know personally.”

“I won’t recruit anyone I’m close to,” said Si-Jie.

Her supervisor looked at her. “Good.”

Si-Jie smiled. She meant it. Mostly.

Her study was about adult attachment: how people described closeness, dependence, discomfort with intimacy, and what they did when they felt rejected. She was interested in the gap between what people said they wanted and how they actually behaved, and her supervisor had warned her twice not to treat attachment styles as diagnoses.

“People are more complicated than a questionnaire.”

Si-Jie wrote that down. She understood. She really did.

But she also had a boyfriend who answered her messages in the order she’d sent them, knew exactly how much ice she liked in her coffee, and could tell what a stranger did for a living after watching him queue for ten minutes. A boyfriend who, asked how he felt, sometimes told her what he’d done instead.

He was interesting. Scientifically speaking. Very interesting. Unfortunately he was also hers, and she was trying hard to keep those two things in separate files.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday evening Arthur was reading a case report at the desk in his flat when she appeared at his elbow with her laptop, a notebook, three pens and an expression he recognised at once.

“No.”

She stopped. “I haven’t asked anything.”

“You’re carrying research materials.”

“How do you know they’re research materials?”

“You have three pens.”

She looked down at her hand, then back at him. “You’re very observant.”

“Thank you.”

“Can you help me?”

“No.”

She put the laptop down on top of the case report. “Please?”

“Si-Jie.”

“Arthur.”

He looked at her. She smiled. He looked at the laptop, and at the notebook, and gave up. “What do you need?”

She sat on the edge of the desk. “Participants.”

“Recruit them through the approved channels.”

“I am. You’re my boyfriend, which makes you a very convenient participant.”

“That isn’t an ethical justification.”

She laughed, and Arthur, who had spent most of his adult life working out how people behaved under pressure, understood that he was about to become the subject of an experiment run by a twenty-one-year-old psychology student who knew exactly how to get him to do things.

“It’s anonymous,” she said.

“Then how do you know it’s me?”

She blinked. He waited. Her eyes narrowed. “You’re being difficult.”

“I’m asking a reasonable question.”

“Fine. It isn’t anonymous to me. But your answers are confidential, and nothing that identifies you goes anywhere near the write-up.”

“That’s better.”

“So you’ll do it?”

“I didn’t say that.”

She slid a consent form across the desk. Arthur looked at it. “Have you had ethics approval?”

“On Tuesday.”

“Has your supervisor approved the final questionnaire?”

“Yes.”

“Can participants withdraw?”

She smiled in triumph. “At any point before the data’s anonymised and goes into the analysis, under the approved procedure. I know my research ethics.”

He picked up the form. “Clearly. Explain what you’re asking me to do.”

Her face changed. She’d expected teasing, not that. She told him what the study was for, how long it would take, how the answers would be stored, and that none of them were right or wrong. Arthur listened. He read the form to the end, and signed it.

Si-Jie looked at the signature. “You signed.”

“Yes.”

She grinned at him. “You’re participating. Thank you.”

“Don’t look so pleased.”

“I am pleased,” she said, and gathered her papers.

He went back to his report.

At the door she stopped. “Arthur? Please answer honestly.”

He looked up. “I always do.”

“That’s what I’m afraid of,” said Si-Jie.

✦ ✦ ✦

He filled it in on Sunday evening at the dining table, two days after Valentine’s Day, with Si-Jie opposite him. She’d promised not to look at his answers. She was keeping her promise. Mostly.

“Don’t look,” he said.

“I’m not.”

“You’re looking.”

“I’m looking at the table.”

“The questionnaire is on the table.”

She looked at the ceiling. “Fine.”

The statements were about comfort with closeness, relying on other people, fear of being left and saying what you need. He answered slowly, not because he didn’t understand them but because he wanted his answers to be accurate. Some were straightforward. Others took longer. He stopped at one.

I find it relatively easy to get close to other people.

He considered the wording, and chose. Si-Jie was watching his face. “What’s taking so long?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re thinking.”

“That’s generally how questionnaires work.”

She laughed. A few minutes later he stopped again.

I am comfortable depending on other people.

He looked at the options, then at the statement, and his pen stayed where it was. Si-Jie noticed, and didn’t ask. She’d learned that Arthur sometimes needed time for questions that seemed simple to everyone else. Eventually he marked an answer, and she went back to studying the ceiling.

He turned the page to question nine, read it and looked up. “Your wording is interesting.”

Si-Jie sat up at once. “Which one?”

He turned the questionnaire round so that she could read it.

She frowned at the statement. “What’s wrong with it?”

“Nothing.”

“Then what?”

He put his pen down. “You want to know whether I’m comfortable with emotional intimacy.”

“Among other things.”

“And you’re asking me to choose an option.”

“Yes.”

He looked at her. “It depends on the person.”

“That’s why it’s a questionnaire,” she said, smiling.

“That doesn’t make the answer any less dependent on context.”

She leaned across the table. “Arthur, please don’t start debating my methodology.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He read the statement once more, chose, and put the pen down. “Finished.”

She reached for the papers.

He didn’t let go straight away. “Are you going to analyse my answers?”

“Only as part of the approved research process.”

“Not personally?”

She looked at him. “Not as a way of judging you.”

He studied her face, and let go. “Good.”

“Thank you, participant Kao,” she said.

He went back to his report. “You’re welcome, researcher Yen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By Monday her research had a problem, and it wasn’t the research. The questionnaires were coming back. The data was being organised. Her supervisor was pleased. But she kept thinking about one particular participant: not because his answers were unusual, or because she wanted to prove anything about him, but because she knew the person behind them.

She knew Arthur could be affectionate in private and reserved in public. That he could spend hours with her without saying much and still remember every word. That he hardly ever asked for reassurance, and always noticed when she needed it. That being the centre of someone’s attention made him uneasy when the attention was about his feelings. And that he’d once held a lift in Hong Kong for an extra minute because he wasn’t ready to let go of her.

She looked at the questionnaire, and then at her notes, and reminded herself that what she knew about him wasn’t data. A participant’s answers weren’t a diagnosis. A questionnaire could show a pattern. It couldn’t tell her everything about a person. She wrote it in her notebook.

A measure isn’t the person.

She underlined it twice. Her phone buzzed.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Have you eaten?

Si-Jie: Not yet.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): It’s nearly five.

Si-Jie: I’m working.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): That doesn’t answer my question.

Si-Jie: You’re very concerned about food.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): You’re very bad at remembering it.

She laughed into her sleeve, two floors up in the library, and looked at his questionnaire again before she typed.

Si-Jie: I’ll eat. I’ve got a question about your answers. Can I ask you later?

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Yes.

Si-Jie: Not as a researcher.

There was a pause.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Then as what?

Si-Jie: Your girlfriend.

His reply came almost at once.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): That sounds more dangerous.

She laughed out loud in the silent section, and the boy at the next desk glared at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday night she was supposed to be writing her literature review. She’d been sitting at the end of his desk for twenty minutes and had written three sentences, and she’d spent most of that time watching him.

“Arthur.”

“Hm?”

“Do you remember question nine?”

He looked up. “Yes.”

“What did you think of it?”

“I thought it was broad.”

She frowned. “That isn’t what I mean.”

“What do you mean?”

She closed her laptop and turned her chair to face him. “Do you find it easy to let someone get close to you?”

“That’s not the exact wording.”

“I know. I’m not asking as a researcher any more.”

“All right,” he said, and leaned back.

She waited.

“Not particularly.”

She nodded. “Why?”

“Because I’m used to managing things myself.”

“Everything?”

“Most things.”

“Even when you’re tired?”

“Being tired doesn’t change who’s responsible.”

She studied him. “Why?”

He was quiet for a while. “It’s easier to be responsible for something when you don’t have to depend on anyone else.”

Si-Jie looked down. She understood that answer, perhaps better than he knew. “Does that mean you don’t want anyone to depend on you either?”

He reached for her hand. “No. That’s different.”

“How?”

“I don’t mind being responsible for someone I care about.”

“Even if it’s difficult?”

“Yes.”

“Even if they need you?”

“Yes.”

She smiled a little. “You’re very good at taking care of people.”

“That’s not the same as letting them take care of me.”

She went quiet, and then moved her chair closer. “Can I?”

He watched her. “Can you what?”

She put her hand against his cheek. “Take care of you. Not all the time. Not in every way. Just sometimes.”

He didn’t answer at once. When he did, his face had gone gentle. “Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and leaned in and kissed him.

It was meant to be a small kiss, a gentle one. But Arthur caught her hand before she could pull away. “Wait.”

She blinked. “What?”

“You asked me a question. I haven’t finished answering it.”

“Then answer.”

He stood. She stayed in her chair, and he stepped in between her knees with one hand on the edge of the desk. “Question nine.”

“Yes,” she said.

He bent his head until his forehead touched hers, and then he kissed her, slowly. She smiled against his mouth and didn’t open her eyes. He kissed her again, and she reached for his shirt.

“Arthur. You’re supposed to use words.”

He looked at her. “I’ve used enough words.”

He kissed her once more, and she laughed against his mouth and put her hands on his shoulders, and he drew her closer. The questionnaire lay on the desk beside them. Her laptop was still open on half a literature review. None of it seemed important for the next few minutes.

When he finally drew back he kept his forehead against hers. Si-Jie smiled. “You’re avoiding the question.”

“No.”

“Yes.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheek. “I’m comfortable being close to you.”

Her face softened. “You mean that?”

“Yes.”

“Even emotionally?”

He looked at her. “That’s the part I didn’t expect.”

She didn’t say anything. She kissed him again instead.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday morning his questionnaire was in the folder on the dining table, ready to hand in. She picked the folder up, and stopped. She’d promised not to analyse him outside the research. She’d also promised herself not to read his answers as a private explanation for everything he’d ever done. So she put it down again.

Arthur came into the kitchen. “Looking for something?”

She turned round. “No.”

He looked at the folder, and then at her. “You’re curious.”

“Of course I’m curious.”

“Researcher?”

She smiled. “Girlfriend.”

He came over and took the folder out of her hands. “Then you can ask me.”

“Ask you what?”

“Whatever you want to know.”

She thought about it. “Do you ever feel lonely?”

Arthur didn’t answer straight away. It was a different question from the ones in the folder: much simpler, and perhaps harder. “Sometimes.”

She nodded. “Do you tell anyone?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“I didn’t used to think there was a reason to.”

She stepped closer. “And now?”

He put the folder down. “Now I have you.”

Her face went soft, and she took his hand. “That’s not a very scientific answer.”

“No.”

“Not very detailed, either.”

“No.”

“You’re getting better at this,” she said, smiling.

“At what?”

“Answering.”

He drew her in. “Then I have another answer.”

“What?”

He kissed her temple. “I miss you when you’re not here.”

“Even when I’m only at university?”

“Yes.”

“Even when I send you forty messages?”

“The forty messages are how I know you’re coming back.”

She laughed, and put her arms round him and held on. “That’s my favourite answer.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine that evening Arthur answered the messages she’d sent him during the day. There were thirty-two. One was a photograph of her lunch. One was a complaint about her supervisor. One was a dog in a yellow raincoat. One said only:

Si-Jie: I think my boyfriend is an interesting research subject.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Your boyfriend thinks his researcher is biased.

She answered at once, sitting up in bed.

Si-Jie: I am not biased.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): You kissed the participant during data collection.

Si-Jie stared at the screen, and burst out laughing.

Si-Jie: THAT WAS NOT DATA COLLECTION.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Understood.

Si-Jie: It was a personal question.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): I answered it.

Si-Jie: With your mouth.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): You seemed satisfied with the response.

She put her face in the pillow for a while. Then she typed.

Si-Jie: Good night, Arthur.

His reply came a moment later.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): Good night, researcher.

She lay there smiling at the ceiling. Somewhere between the ethics forms and the questionnaires and the questions neither of them had known how to ask before, she’d learned something her thesis wasn’t going to cover.

Closeness wasn’t always loud. Sometimes it was a hand reaching across a dining table. A message answered at nine. A man who’d spent his life depending on nobody, learning, slowly, to say when he missed someone.

And sometimes it was a question left unanswered on a desk, because the person sitting across from you had already found another way to answer it.

chapters.title: Valentine’s, Measured
chapters.desc: Valentine’s Day by spreadsheet: white tulips, a silver star, a table at a quarter past eight. She removes a variable: his tie, and then his hands. Up to the bedroom door, not explicit.
chapters.content:
Arthur Kao prepared for Valentine’s Day with the seriousness he brought to a criminal investigation. There was a spreadsheet. It had six columns: item, preference, evidence, probability of enjoyment, acquisition status and notes.

Flowers · white tulips · mentioned twice, photographed once · high
Chocolate · dark, not too bitter · previous purchase · high
Dinner · Japanese · favourite restaurant, three references · high
Dessert · strawberry shortcake · repeated preference · high
Gift · silver necklace · stopped at a jeweller’s window, 26 January · high

Under it were the notes. Avoid red roses: she’d once called them too dramatic. No perfume: her preferences were specific, and choosing blind carried unnecessary risk. No surprise guests. No restaurant with loud music. A table by the window. Transport arranged. Her university timetable confirmed.

At the bottom he’d written two lines.

Primary objective: make Si-Jie happy.
Secondary objective: avoid unnecessary variables.

At five on Friday afternoon his phone buzzed.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Are you busy?

Arthur: No.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): What are you doing?

Arthur: Preparing something.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Is it classified?

Arthur: No.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Can I know?

Arthur: No.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): That’s suspicious.

Arthur: You asked whether it was classified. I answered.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): You’re being very technical today.

Arthur looked at the spreadsheet, and then at the message.

Arthur: I have always been technical.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Not when you kiss me.

He put the phone in the desk drawer and shut it. For the first time that day, he considered that his plan might have a weakness.

✦ ✦ ✦

She arrived eight minutes early, in a soft pink dress under her coat, with her hair loose over her shoulders and a paper bag in her hand. Arthur opened the door and looked at her, and then at the bag.

“What’s that?”

“Something for you.”

“I thought we’d agreed I was arranging tonight.”

“We did.”

“Then why did you bring something?”

“Because I wanted to.”

He stepped aside. She came in, took off her shoes and put the bag on the kitchen counter, and before he could ask what was in it she turned round and wrapped both arms round his waist.

“Happy Valentine’s Day.”

Arthur looked down at her. “Happy Valentine’s Day.”

She waited. He didn’t move.

“That’s it?”

“What else?”

“You’re supposed to kiss me.”

“I was going to.”

“You were taking too long,” she said, and pulled him down by his collar and kissed him.

His hand settled on her back. He kissed her with the familiar restraint that never quite lasted when she was involved, and when she let go she was smiling.

“Better.”

“You’re early.”

“By eight minutes.”

“I noticed.”

“Of course you did.”

He took her coat and hung it up. She wandered into the living room, where white tulips stood in a glass vase on the dining table, and stopped.

“Oh.”

Arthur watched her face.

“White tulips,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You remembered.”

“You told me you liked them.”

“That was three weeks ago.”

“Twenty-six days.”

She turned round slowly. “Arthur. You’re very romantic.”

“I made a reservation.”

She laughed. He glanced at her, and she shook her head. “You’re just so serious about it.”

“Would you prefer an unplanned evening?”

“No.”

“Good.”

She touched one of the petals with a fingertip. “They’re beautiful.”

He watched her a moment longer than he needed to. The spreadsheet had predicted she would like the flowers. It hadn’t accounted for the way her face changed when she realised he’d kept something she’d said without thinking. That was an inconvenient omission.

“There’s more,” he said, and gave her a small box.

Inside was a fine silver necklace with a tiny, plain star. Si-Jie stared at it, and then at him. “You bought me jewellery?”

“Yes.”

“You saw me looking at it?”

“You stopped in front of the window.”

“I didn’t even say I wanted it.”

“You didn’t have to.”

She closed the box and held it against her chest. “Will you put it on me?”

He took the necklace out. She turned round and lifted her hair, and his fingers brushed the back of her neck as he fastened the clasp.

“Done.”

She didn’t turn straight away. She reached up and touched the pendant.

“Do you like it?” he asked.

“I love it.”

“Good.”

She turned, took his hand and kissed his knuckles.

Arthur looked down at their hands. “That’s not necessary.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

“Because I love you.”

He went still. Not because he didn’t know what to say, but because he did. He lifted her hand and kissed the same place. “I love you too.”

Her smile was impossibly pleased. “See? That’s a good Valentine’s Day.”

“We haven’t had dinner yet.”

“You’re right. There’s still room for improvement.”

He narrowed his eyes at her, and she laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner went exactly to plan. The restaurant was quiet. The table was by the window. The food was what she liked, and the shortcake came with a small candle that she insisted they blow out together.

He’d worked out the schedule with reasonable precision. Dinner at a quarter past eight. Dessert at ten past nine. Home by ten.

He hadn’t planned for her to feed him the last spoonful of cake. He hadn’t planned for her to steal his hand under the table, or to spend the taxi ride home leaning on his shoulder and lifting her head every so often just to look at him.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“I’m looking.”

“There’s a difference?”

“Yes.”

“Explain.”

“Staring is rude. Looking at your boyfriend is romantic.”

“A convenient distinction.”

She smiled and settled against him again. When they got in he checked the time. Six minutes past ten: six minutes behind schedule, a negligible deviation. He took off his watch and put it on the bedside table.

Si-Jie was in front of the mirror, looking at the necklace. “Arthur? Did you plan everything?”

“Most of it.”

“Most?”

“I left some room for adjustment.”

She turned. “Adjustment?”

“If you wanted something different.”

She considered him, and smiled in a way he’d learned to recognise as dangerous. “Actually, I do.”

“What?”

She came towards him. “Something different.”

“Such as?”

She stopped in front of him with both hands on his chest and looked up. “Can I ask you something?”

“You can.”

“Do you know how many times you’ve looked at the clock tonight?”

“Seven.”

“Seven?”

“Eight, including now.”

She laughed. “You’re unbelievable.”

“Is that the adjustment?”

“No,” she said, and reached for his tie.

Arthur glanced down at her fingers. “What are you doing?”

“Removing a variable.”

“Which one?”

“You.”

She tugged the knot loose and drew the tie out from under his collar. Arthur’s expression stayed composed. “Si-Jie. You’re holding my tie.”

“I noticed.”

“Why?”

She looped it round her fingers. “Because I have a plan.”

He regarded her for a moment. “That’s rarely reassuring.”

She laughed and kissed him. This time he didn’t take the kiss over. He let her set the pace. He let her hands move over his shoulders and draw him closer until the careful distance between them was gone.

When she pulled back she was smiling. “Can I tie your hands?”

Arthur looked at the tie, and then at her. “With my tie?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“So you can’t keep checking things.”

“I don’t check things while—”

“Arthur.”

He stopped. She raised an eyebrow, and he studied her face, looking for hesitation, or making sure she meant it.

“You’re certain?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me if you want me to stop.”

“I will.”

He held her gaze a second longer, and lifted his hands. “All right.”

She tied his wrists with his own tie, gently, to the bedpost, loosely enough that he could move. She checked the knot and looked at him. “Too tight?”

“No.”

“Can you move?”

“Yes.”

She sat down beside him and tilted her head. “Good. Now what?”

Arthur looked at the tie round his wrists, and then at her. “You tell me.”

Her smile widened. It was a strange experience, not being able to reach for her. He was used to knowing where his hands were and what they were doing, used to making small corrections before anyone else saw a problem. Now his hands were occupied, and Si-Jie was looking at him as though she’d discovered something wonderful.

“You’re thinking,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“Stop.”

“That’s not how thinking works.”

She kissed him. He tried to answer, and she kissed him again. “You’re still thinking.”

“You’re making it difficult not to.”

“Good.”

She ran her fingers along his cheek and kissed the corner of his mouth, and he watched her closely. There was no spreadsheet now. No sequence, no probability, no reasonable forecast of what she’d do next. Only Si-Jie: her fingers in his hair, her laughter against his mouth, the warmth of her as she leaned in. He’d thought he understood the difference between being restrained and being unable to act. He was beginning to understand that it mattered a good deal less when he trusted the person holding the tie.

“Arthur? Do you want me to untie you?”

He looked at her. “No.”

Her face softened. “No?”

“Not yet.”

She kissed him again, and when she drew back he followed as far as the tie allowed. She laughed. “You’re impatient.”

“An observation.”

“You’re not supposed to make observations.”

“Then stop giving me evidence.”

She covered his mouth with hers, and at last he stopped talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later the bedroom was quiet. The tie lay folded on the bedside table beside his watch. His phone hadn’t been looked at in nearly two hours. Si-Jie lay beside him with one hand over his chest, and he was looking at the ceiling.

She turned her head. “Are you thinking about your spreadsheet?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

“I’m reviewing the evening.”

“That’s worse.”

He glanced at her. “Your behaviour was not consistent with the expected schedule.”

She laughed into his shoulder. “Sorry.”

“You don’t sound sorry.”

“I’m not.”

“I noticed.”

She came up on one elbow. “Did you have a good Valentine’s Day?”

“Yes.”

“Even though I ruined your plan?”

“Your contribution wasn’t entirely negative.”

“Not entirely?”

He looked at her. “It was considerably better than expected.”

She smiled. “That’s the most romantic thing you’ve ever said.”

“It isn’t.”

“What’s more romantic?”

He thought about it. Then he took her hand and brought it to his lips. “I’d have wanted you here even if I hadn’t planned anything.”

She went still.

Arthur looked at her. “That’s the answer you wanted?”

She nodded.

He brushed his thumb over her knuckles. “Then you should have asked.”

“I wanted you to say it without being asked.”

“An unreasonable experimental condition.”

“Arthur.”

“But I understand.”

She smiled and put her head down on his chest. After a while she spoke again. “Can I see the spreadsheet?”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Confidential.”

“To whom?”

“You.”

She lifted her head. “How can something about me be confidential from me?”

“Because you’d interfere with the data.”

“I already did.”

“Exactly.”

She laughed. Then he remembered the paper bag on the kitchen counter, which nobody had opened.

“What was in the bag?”

“Go and look.”

He got up and went to look. Inside, wrapped in tissue paper, was a tie: dark blue silk, plainer and better than any of his. He brought it back to the bedroom and held it up.

“You bought me a tie.”

“To replace the one I was going to ruin.”

He looked at the folded tie on the bedside table, and then at the new one, and then at her. “You planned it.”

“I left some room for adjustment,” said Si-Jie, with great dignity, and pulled the covers up to her nose so he wouldn’t see her laughing.

He got back into bed. She reached across him for her phone and typed. A moment later his own phone buzzed on the bedside table. He picked it up.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Valentine’s Day evaluation.

Arthur: Go on.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Flowers: 10/10.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Necklace: 100/10.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Dinner: 10/10.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Boyfriend: 100000/10.

Arthur: Inflated score.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): No. Scientifically accurate.

Arthur: Your methodology is questionable.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): My methodology is kissing you until you stop arguing.

Arthur put the phone down.

She was watching him. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

He turned towards her, took her chin gently and kissed her. When he drew back she looked thoroughly satisfied.

“See?”

“An effective method,” he conceded.

She settled against him again. Arthur reached over and switched off the lamp, and for the first time that evening he didn’t know what time it was, and didn’t particularly care.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near midnight he opened his laptop. Si-Jie was asleep beside him with her hand still resting against his ribs. He opened the spreadsheet, and under the final notes he added a line.

Control condition: failed.

He paused, and added another.

Cause: subject refused to behave according to predicted variables.

He looked at her. Her hair was spread across his pillow. The silver star lay against her collarbone. Her breathing was slow and even. He turned back to the screen.

Conclusion: the experiment was successful.

A moment passed. He changed the last line.

Conclusion: no further study required.

He closed the laptop, moved closer and gathered her carefully against him, and pressed a kiss to her temple. The spreadsheet had been useful. It had helped him remember the flowers, the necklace, the restaurant and the dessert. But it had never been able to account for the most important part: that he could plan an entire evening around making her happy, and still find the best moment was the one he hadn’t planned at all.

Si-Jie stirred. “Arthur?”

“Go back to sleep.”

She reached for him without opening her eyes, and he took her hand.

“Happy Valentine’s Day,” he whispered.

She smiled against his chest. “Happy Valentine’s Day.”

And for once, Arthur Kao let the night go unmeasured.

chapters.title: The Notebook
chapters.desc: Looking for a charging cable, she finds his notebook: her name on every page since the seminar, what she eats, when she cries. Am I a case? He won’t call her one, and that isn’t quite the same promise.
chapters.content:
Si-Jie had learned that Arthur’s flat had two kinds of space.

The first kind belonged to both of them. The kitchen, where she had a favourite mug. The bathroom, where her toothbrush stood beside his. The bedroom, where one drawer had gradually become hers, though Arthur maintained it had been allocated for practical reasons.

The second kind belonged only to Arthur. His workroom was one of them: a small room at the end of the hall with a desk, two bookcases, a filing cabinet and a chair she’d once described as having been chosen to discourage human happiness. He’d told her it was comfortable. She’d told him that was evidence of questionable judgement.

On Wednesday night in the middle of March he was in the shower, and she was looking for a charging cable.

She knew where he kept the spare ones: second drawer of the desk, on the left. She’d opened it before, with his permission, and found everything in small compartments. She pulled it open now. Cable. Adapter. Spare batteries. And under a thin folder, a black notebook.

It was unremarkable. A black leather cover with no title and no label, the corners a little worn from being carried. She’d seen it in his inside pocket a hundred times and assumed it was for work.

She picked it up and opened it, and saw her name.

YEN SI-JIE
16 October 2024

The day they’d met. She stood still, and turned the page.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first entries were from the seminar.

Second row, beside the girl with the notebook (Eliana Lin).
Forty questions. I answered thirty-nine.
Maintained eye contact throughout. Appeared amused by my answers.
Not discouraged by the lack of encouragement.
Followed me to the staff car park at dusk. Her sisters held her bag.
Question forty: whether she could kiss me. Asked before she touched me.
Subject appeared surprised when I kissed her back.
Question forty-one: my number.

Subject. Si-Jie swallowed, and kept reading.

17 October. Sixth floor, 10.18. Brought breakfast.
Answered all eleven reasons. Didn’t accept the first refusal to discuss personal matters.
Asked whether I didn’t want her, or was afraid.
Unusually perceptive.

28 October. Approximately forty messages. Breakfast, a lecture, a cat, an umbrella, a cloud, a stranger’s shoes. None needed an answer. Answered all at nine. She was pleased.

23 November. Met her sisters. Si-Wei is direct and distrusts authority. Si-Yuan is more observant than she lets people see.
Si-Jie angry when I spoke about Si-Wei’s private life at the table. I apologised.
She kissed me against the lamp post outside her building. She was still angry.
Accepted the apology after approximately eleven minutes.
She doesn’t stop being affectionate when upset.

It wasn’t a collection of occasional notes. It was a record, nearly daily, some entries a line long and some a page, and every one of them was about her.

2 November. Iced oat latte, less ice, no syrup. Left a third. Said she was full. Ate half my dessert. Denied taking more than half.

14 November. Cried at a documentary. Tried to hide it. Said she wasn’t crying. Accepted a tissue. Didn’t want to discuss it.
Don’t ask straight away. Wait until she is ready.

Her fingers tightened on the page.

When anxious, talks faster and becomes precise about small details.
When upset, stops asking questions and starts making statements.
When uncomfortable, touches her left earring.
When she is really happy, she gets quieter. Lets a conversation stop without rushing to rescue it.

Her hand had gone up to her left earring. She took it down.

13 December. Twenty-one. Afternoon with her sisters; she saved the candle from their cake. Dinner with me. Wore the chain at the table.
Keep this date clear in future years.

14 December. Hong Kong. My mother held both her hands.
In the lift she held me for nine floors and didn’t let go when the doors opened.
Asked whether my parents hug me. I said no. She held me again.
I didn’t ask her to stop.

She remembered that lift. The way he’d stood so stiffly at first, as though he didn’t know what to do with her arms round him. The way he’d reached past her and held the doors, and asked for another minute.

17 January. Home at 3.08. She was asleep on the sofa. Had waited although I told her not to.
Didn’t ask about the case. Held me without speaking.
She doesn’t need me to explain everything.
I should still tell her when I will be late.

14 February. White tulips. Silver necklace, star. Table at 8.15. Strawberry shortcake.
She liked the necklace. She liked the flowers. She changed the order of the evening.
Tied my hands with my own tie.
I didn’t anticipate how much I would enjoy that.

Her face went hot, even with the cold beginning to settle in her stomach.

15 February. Woke at 8.12. Stole strawberries from my plate. Said she loved me at the door. Came back three minutes later for her phone.
She hadn’t forgotten it. It was on the kitchen counter.

9 March. Dinner. She asked whether I ever get tired of listening to people. I said no. She seemed relieved. She didn’t ask why.

At the back there was a second section, the same handwriting, arranged under headings.

SLEEP. Sleeps later when studying. Falls asleep faster close to someone. Wakes when the room goes too quiet. Denies being tired until she is already asleep.
FOOD. Skips breakfast when anxious. Eats more slowly when upset. Strawberries. Dislikes sweet drinks. Says she is full before she has finished.
DISTRESS. Cries alone when overwhelmed. Makes a joke straight afterwards. Doesn’t always want to discuss the cause. Ask whether she wants company or space.
TOWARDS ME. Starts most of the affection. Notices changes in my mood. Not intimidated by my work. Finds it hard to accept I may not be able to answer every question. Asks anyway.

Underneath, two more lines.

I have become accustomed to her presence.
Absence is now noticeable.

The second was underlined. Si-Jie closed the notebook, and heard the shower stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Arthur came down the hall in a dark shirt, drying his hair. “Have you seen my—”

He stopped. She was standing by his desk with the black notebook in her hands. He looked at it, and then at her, and for several seconds neither of them said anything. He put the towel down.

“Si-Jie.”

“How long?”

“Since the seminar.”

She gave a small laugh that had nothing to do with being amused. “You’ve been writing about me since the day we met?”

“Yes.”

“Every day?”

“Almost.”

“Almost?”

“There are some days without a separate entry.”

She looked at him like a stranger who’d learned her name. She opened the notebook and held it up. “You wrote down what I eat.”

“Yes.”

“When I cry. How long I sleep. What I do when I’m upset. How I react when you touch me. How many messages I send. You even wrote down how long I took to accept your apology.”

“Approximately eleven minutes.”

“Don’t.”

He stopped. Her fingers were trembling.

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to understand you.”

“Is that what you call this?”

He glanced at the notebook. “I recorded observations.”

She looked down at the pages, and back up. “Observations. Am I a case?”

The question lay between them. She wanted him to laugh, to tell her she’d misunderstood, to take the notebook out of her hands and explain that it was something harmless, something that had nothing to do with the way he looked at the people he investigated. She wanted him to say she was different. But Arthur didn’t lie.

“No. Not in the professional sense.”

Her face changed. “What’s the difference?”

“I have no investigative interest in you.”

“But you have a record.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve written down everything.”

“Not everything.”

She looked at him, and he heard it too late. He’d chosen the wrong words, and knowing it didn’t make the correction any easier.

“Si-Jie—”

She held up the notebook. “Do you know what this looks like? It looks like a file. The kind you’d make about someone you were investigating. Someone whose behaviour you wanted to predict.”

He didn’t deny it. “I understand.”

“No, you don’t.”

“Then explain it to me.”

She laughed once, without any warmth in it. “That’s what you always do. You ask questions. You watch. You write things down. You turn everything into something you can understand. And what about me? What about the fact that I didn’t know?”

He looked at her. “I should have told you. I didn’t, and I won’t pretend otherwise.”

She looked down at the pages. There was something worse than the notebook itself. He’d been doing this while he held her. While he kissed her. While he told her he loved her. He’d watched her cry, and written it down. He’d learned her the way he learned a pattern of behaviour, and she’d never known where the affection stopped and the observation began.

“Was any of it real?”

Something moved in his face, almost too small to see. “Yes.”

“How can I know?”

“You can’t.”

Her head came up.

He held her gaze. “I can tell you what it means to me. I can’t decide what you’re supposed to feel about it.”

She couldn’t speak. That was the worst part. He wasn’t trying to persuade her, or to make it sound beautiful. He was standing there telling her the truth.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Why did you start?”

“You were unusual. You asked questions I didn’t expect. You were direct. You didn’t seem to mind whether I liked you. After you’d gone I remembered things about you, and I wrote them down, because I wanted to remember.”

“Then why keep doing it?”

He took a breath. It was a small thing, and she’d learned to notice it. Arthur hardly ever had to prepare himself to speak.

“At first it was habit.”

“Your work.”

“Yes.”

“And later?”

“Later I wanted to know you.”

“Then why didn’t you just ask me?”

“I did. Not about this, because I didn’t know how to explain it.”

She shook her head. “You can explain a murder scene to a whole task force, and you can’t tell your girlfriend you’ve been keeping a notebook about her?”

“That’s an accurate assessment.”

She almost laughed. Almost. He took a step towards her, and she took a step back. He stopped at once. The movement was small, and of course he noticed it.

“Do you know what scares me? That you know so much about me, and I didn’t even know you were collecting it,” she said.

“I wasn’t collecting you.”

“You were recording me. Without asking.”

“Yes.”

“Do you read it?”

“Not every day.”

“Arthur.”

“When I miss something about you.”

She looked up. He didn’t explain, and he didn’t need to. When she wasn’t there, he could open the notebook and find her: her breakfast, her laughter, her tears. A version of her that couldn’t surprise him, because he’d already written down what she might do.

“You can remember me without writing me down.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

His jaw tightened. For the first time he couldn’t seem to find a precise answer. “Because remembering you became important to me.”

“That doesn’t make it all right.”

“No.”

He didn’t defend himself, and she hated that she was grateful.

She put the notebook down on the desk, carefully, like something that didn’t belong to her. “Do you think I’m predictable?”

“No. That’s why I wrote it down. Your reactions change. Your preferences change. Sometimes you say one thing and mean another. You can be upset and still want me close. You can be happy and go quiet. You decide things before you explain them.”

“You make it sound like a list of faults.”

“It’s a list of things I wanted to understand.”

“You’re still talking about me like something to study.”

He was silent. The room felt small.

“Does anyone else know?”

“No. Not my colleagues and not my family. I’ve never used it for work. I’ve never compared you to a subject. I haven’t used it to manipulate you, and I haven’t made decisions about you because of it.”

“But you decided to keep it. Without me.”

“Yes.”

She nodded slowly. It wasn’t relief. It was only another set of answers. “Can I read the rest?”

“Yes. All of it. I won’t stop you, and there’s nothing in it I don’t want you to see.”

She picked the notebook up again, and didn’t open it. “Not tonight.”

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t go to bed for a long time. She sat on the sofa with her legs folded under her, and he sat in the armchair opposite. He didn’t try to touch her. She didn’t ask him to leave. The notebook lay on the coffee table between them.

At last she spoke. “Do you know what I remember about you? I don’t have a notebook. But I remember that you take your coffee black. That you check the lock twice before bed. That you don’t like people standing behind you. That you don’t sleep after a bad case. That you hold my hand when you think I’m asleep. That you buy strawberries even though you don’t like them nearly as much as I do.”

“I don’t dislike strawberries.”

She looked at him. “You don’t like them enough to buy that many. I remember all of it because I love you. Not because I want to understand you like a problem. That’s why this hurts.”

He took that without answering.

“When you look at me now, what do you see?”

“You.”

“Not the notebook?”

“No.”

“Then look at me. Without trying to work out what I’m thinking. Don’t read my face. Don’t count how long I’m quiet. Don’t write down what happens tonight.”

“I won’t.”

She looked at him. Then she got up, took the notebook off the table and held it against her chest. “I’m taking this to bed. Not because I’ve forgiven you. Because I want to read it.”

“All right.”

She went towards the hall, and he didn’t follow. At the bedroom door she stopped. “Arthur? Are you coming?”

“Do you want me to?”

She hesitated, and nodded. He got up, and when he reached her he didn’t touch her. She looked at his hands, and then at his face.

“Can you hold me?”

“Yes,” he said, and put his arms round her.

She rested her forehead against his chest. “I don’t want to be your case.”

“You’re not.”

“Promise?”

“I won’t call you one.”

She closed her eyes. It wasn’t quite the same promise, and they both knew it. Tonight she was too tired to ask for a better one.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past one she was still awake, with the notebook on her side of the bed. She’d read more. Some of it was ordinary. Some of it was almost unbearably intimate: the way she hummed while she brushed her teeth, the way she rubbed her thumb along the edge of her phone when she was anxious, the way she always reached for him crossing a road even when there were no cars. Dates she’d forgotten. Small moments Arthur had kept.

She turned to him. “Did you write down the first time I told you I loved you?”

“Yes. That you said it as a joke, about strawberries. That I wasn’t ready to say it back. That I wanted to be.”

“And the first time you said it?”

He was quiet a moment. “That it was no longer a difficult thing to say.”

She closed the notebook. “If I stop being predictable, will you still want me?”

He turned to face her. “I don’t want you because I can predict you. When you’re here, I want you here. When you’re not, I miss you. When you’re upset, I want to know whether you need me. And when you change your mind, I want to know the new answer.”

Her eyes filled. “That’s a terrible explanation.”

“I know.”

She laughed, and a tear ran down her cheek. Arthur caught it with his thumb. He didn’t record it. He didn’t count. He wiped it away.

“Don’t write this down.”

“I won’t.”

“Don’t remember it as data. Just remember it.”

He held her hand. “I will.”

She kissed him. It wasn’t like before: no teasing, no trying to make him lose his composure. It was a careful kiss, a question, and he answered it by resting his forehead against hers. Then she turned off the lamp, and the notebook stayed shut.

For the first time since the seminar there was something about Si-Jie that Arthur hadn’t written down, and he didn’t know what she’d do next. He lay awake beside her and listened to her breathing. He didn’t count the minutes. He didn’t open the notebook. He stayed.

chapters.title: Partner or Experiment
chapters.desc: Partner or experiment? He says he doesn’t know, and she leaves in the middle of the night. He follows the taxi and doesn’t go up. Her sisters, across three clocks. Fourteen days of silence.
chapters.content:
The notebook was still on the bed. Si-Jie had closed it an hour before, but she hadn’t put it away, and it lay between them with its black cover facing up. Neither of them had slept. Arthur was on his back with one arm at his side. Si-Jie was turned towards the window, watching the faint reflection of the room in the glass, and thinking about a question.

It was a simple one. She’d asked him complicated things before: about his childhood, his family, his work, his feelings. Questions he didn’t want to answer and questions he hadn’t known how to answer. This one should have been easy.

“Arthur. Which one am I?”

He turned his head. “What?”

“Your partner or your experiment?”

He didn’t answer. She waited.

“Si-Jie—”

She glanced at the black cover. “No. Don’t explain the notebook again. I understand why you started it. I understand what you say it means to you. But I need to know which one I am.”

He sat up a little. “You’re my partner.”

“Then why couldn’t you say that earlier?”

His face changed. She’d found the part of the conversation he’d hoped she would leave alone. When she’d asked whether she was a case he’d said no: that she wasn’t a subject, that he’d never used it against her, that it wasn’t evidence. None of it had touched the question underneath.

“Because I don’t know where the distinction began. When I met you I observed you. That was familiar. I remembered details and recorded them, and I went on doing it after we started seeing each other,” he said carefully.

“And after you fell in love with me?”

He didn’t answer at once.

She gave a small nod. “Right.”

“Si-Jie.”

“Do you know when you stopped observing me as a subject and started knowing me as someone you love?”

Arthur looked at her. “I don’t know.”

The room went quiet. He’d answered honestly, and somehow honesty had become the thing that hurt most.

“Then maybe you don’t know me either.”

“That isn’t true.”

Her eyes had begun to shine. “How can you be sure? Because you know what I eat, how I sleep, when I cry, what I do when I’m anxious? Those are things you can write down. They’re not the same as knowing me.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He reached for her hand, and she moved it away. He stopped, and looked at the empty space between them for several seconds.

“I don’t know how to answer without giving you an answer I haven’t earned. I don’t want to tell you you’re only my partner if I haven’t understood what I’ve done.”

“I don’t need a convenient answer. I need to know whether you love me as a person, or the way you’ve learned to understand me.”

His jaw tightened. He looked at her, and then he said the one thing she’d been afraid he’d say.

“I don’t know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Si-Jie sat up. Arthur watched her move. “What are you doing?”

“Going home.”

He looked at the clock. It was nearly two. “Now? I’ll drive you.”

“No. I can get a taxi.”

He stood. “You’re upset. You shouldn’t travel alone at this time.”

She turned to face him. “Please don’t do that. Don’t use what you know about me to decide what I should do.”

He went silent. She put on her cardigan, picked up her phone and her bag, and then the notebook.

“Leave it.”

She held it against her chest. “No.”

“All right,” he said, and didn’t try to take it.

Her shoes were by the door where she’d left them. Arthur followed at a distance and stood by the wall while she put them on.

“Can we talk tomorrow? About us.”

She looked at the floor. “I don’t know if I want to talk tomorrow.”

He nodded once. She opened the door, and he didn’t stop her.

“Goodnight, Arthur.”

“Goodnight.”

The door closed, and for the first time since October Arthur was alone in his flat without knowing when she’d come back.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood behind the door for thirty-seven seconds. He knew because he looked at the clock. Then he picked up his keys and went down without a coat, and came out of the lobby as a taxi pulled away. He saw her cardigan through the rear window.

He got into his car and followed, never close enough to worry the driver, never so far back that he lost it. At the second set of lights he thought about ringing her, and didn’t. At the third he thought about a message, and didn’t. He knew the route to her building. He knew which entrance she preferred. He knew she checked her phone the moment she got out of a taxi. He knew too much, and the thought made his hands tighten on the wheel.

The taxi stopped outside her building, and he parked across the road. She paid, stepped onto the pavement and adjusted the strap of her bag. She looked tired. She didn’t look back. He watched her go in, and got out of the car, and stood on the pavement looking at the lit lobby.

He could go up. He could knock and tell her he’d made a mistake: that he hadn’t been able to tell the habit of observing from the wish to remember someone, that the notebook had begun as a record and become something else. He could tell her the flat was too quiet without her. He could tell her he’d followed the taxi because he couldn’t bear to let her leave while he did nothing.

But she’d left his flat after telling him not to decide things for her because of what he knew. Following her to her door would be one more decision made without asking.

He stood there another minute. Then he got back into the car and drove home.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat looked exactly as it had before she left. Her favourite mug stood by the sink. The necklace box was in its drawer. Her cardigan wasn’t on the back of the sofa any more.

He opened the desk drawer. There was an empty space where the notebook had been. He closed it, and opened it again, as if the result might change. It didn’t.

Later he opened their conversation. Forty messages a day: meals, lectures, questions about something she’d read, cats she’d seen in the street, observations with no practical use at all. The last thing she’d sent before coming over was a photograph of a strawberry.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): This one looks like you.

Arthur: Explain.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): It looks serious.

Arthur: It’s a strawberry.

Si-Jie (Question Forty): Exactly.

He looked at it, and locked the phone. He didn’t know what to do with a conversation that had stopped.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine in the morning Si-Jie rang Si-Yuan from the bus. It was two in the morning in Paris, and she’d worked that out, and rang anyway, because it was a family emergency, and when Si-Yuan answered with a script on the floor beside her, Si-Jie told her so. Then she added Si-Wei, who was in Seoul for a week of a course and had been reading, and for a few minutes she let them argue about whether there could be a wedding without a proposal, because it was easier than the next part.

“I found something. Arthur’s notebook, in his desk, last night. I was looking for a charging cable.”

Si-Wei looked up from her tea. “You read it?”

“Every page is about me. Since the seminar. What I eat. When I cry. How long I sleep. Things I said. Things I did. Things I apparently didn’t say.”

“Did he write it for work?” said Si-Wei.

“He says it isn’t work. He says he wanted to understand me.”

Si-Yuan was still on her floor in Paris. “What did you ask him?”

“Whether I was his partner or his experiment.”

“And?”

“He said he didn’t know. So I left.”

“Did he try to stop you?” said Si-Yuan, over the top of Si-Wei swearing under her breath.

“No.”

“Did he follow you?”

Si-Jie stared at the screen. “How do you know?”

“He did, didn’t he?”

“He followed the taxi. He stopped outside my building. He didn’t come up.”

Si-Wei sat forward. “That doesn’t make it better.”

“I know.”

“Has he rung? Sent anything?” said Si-Yuan.

“No.”

Si-Yuan nodded slowly. “Good. At least he stopped himself.”

“That’s a very generous interpretation,” said Si-Wei.

“It isn’t an excuse. It’s a distinction. Whether he keeps to it is another matter,” said Si-Yuan.

The bus went over a bump. Si-Jie looked out of the window at a city in ordinary daylight. “I love him. I don’t want to stop.”

“Nobody’s asking you to,” said Si-Wei, more gently.

Then Si-Yuan laughed, a small startled sound, and both of them looked at her.

“Sorry. It’s just that between the three of us we’ve managed to find men who make simple things extraordinarily difficult.”

Si-Wei stared at her and laughed too. Si-Jie made a noise that was half a laugh and half something else, and wiped her eyes with her sleeve.

“You can love him and still be angry. You can miss him and still not want to see him. You can understand why he did it and still decide it wasn’t acceptable. And you don’t have to make it easier for him because he’s bad at not knowing things,” said Si-Yuan.

“Exactly. Now eat something,” said Si-Wei.

“Why?”

“Because we know you. Did you have breakfast?”

Si-Jie didn’t answer. Both of them looked at her.

“I had coffee.”

“That isn’t breakfast,” said Si-Yuan, and for the first time that morning Si-Jie smiled properly.

She got off the bus two stops early because she couldn’t sit still, and sat on a bench outside the faculty with the notebook on her knees. The handwriting was neat, almost painfully so. There were no suspects in it and no photographs of anything terrible. It was smaller than that, and more personal, and there were no verdicts, which was almost worse. He’d simply been paying attention.

Under the date of their last dinner he’d written that she’d asked whether he ever got tired of listening to people, and that he’d said no, and that she’d seemed relieved and hadn’t asked why. She remembered the evening. She’d been talking too much, jumping from his work to his childhood to his family, and she’d stopped herself and asked, and he’d looked at her and said no, and she’d laughed and changed the subject. She hadn’t known he’d kept it.

She opened their conversation and typed that she had his notebook, and deleted it. She typed a question, why he hadn’t told her, and deleted that too. Then she put the phone away. She was going to make him answer the question properly. Not today.

✦ ✦ ✦

He sent a message at nine that evening.

Arthur: Have you eaten?

It sat there unanswered. A few minutes later he sent another.

Arthur: I won’t ask you to come over. I only wanted to know you’re safe.

No reply came. Later he took a new notebook out of the drawer: black, the same size. He opened it to the first page and held the pen over it for several minutes without writing anything. Then he closed it and put it away.

✦ ✦ ✦

The silence lasted fourteen days. There was no argument with a grand ending: no slammed doors, no long messages at three in the morning that either of them regretted. There was simply no contact. Si-Jie stopped sending forty messages, and Arthur stopped receiving them.

At first he checked his phone at nine out of habit. Then he started checking it at eight, and then at seven. He knew it was irrational, and he did it anyway.

At work Eugene noticed. “You’ve been quiet.”

Arthur didn’t look up from the report. “I’m always quiet.”

“Not like this. Did you and Si-Jie have a fight?”

Arthur’s pen stopped. Eugene raised his eyebrows.

“That serious?”

“Yes.”

“Are you going to fix it?”

“I don’t know.”

Eugene looked at him for a while. “That’s new.”

Arthur closed the file. “I’m aware.”

At home the flat stayed immaculate. No cardigan on the sofa. No hair clip by the basin. No second cup in the kitchen. He hadn’t moved any of her things. Her drawer was untouched, and her toothbrush still stood beside his. He didn’t know whether keeping them was hope, or an inability to accept that she might not come back. He didn’t write it down. He didn’t write anything down.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourteenth night Si-Jie was on another video call, nearly at midnight. Si-Wei was home from Seoul and at her desk across the city. In Paris it was late afternoon, and Si-Yuan was holding up a red linen dress she’d found at a market.

They’d been talking for nearly an hour. Si-Wei was complaining about her group project. Si-Jie was listening, and laughing now and then. Then Si-Wei asked whether she’d heard from him, and her smile went.

“No.”

“Have you contacted him?”

“No.”

“Do you want to?” said Si-Yuan.

Si-Jie thought about it. “Yes. I just don’t know what I’d say.”

“That’s fair,” said Si-Wei.

“Do you think he misses me?”

Neither of them answered at once. Then Si-Yuan nodded. “Yes. He followed your taxi.”

Si-Wei gave her a look. “That’s not necessarily romantic.”

Si-Yuan turned back to the screen. “I didn’t say it was. But he misses you. The question is whether missing you will make him understand what you needed him to understand.”

Si-Jie looked down. Her phone was on the table. She opened their conversation, where his last message was fourteen days old, and read it again.

Arthur (Thirty-Nine): I won’t ask you to come over. I only wanted to know you’re safe.

She locked the phone. “Maybe I need more time.”

“Then take more time,” said Si-Wei.

Si-Yuan smiled a little. “And when you’re ready, make him answer the question properly.”

“Which question?”

“Partner or experiment.”

Si-Jie nodded. Outside, the night went on as usual. Three sisters stayed on the line across two clocks, and on the other side of the city Arthur Kao was awake, looking at a phone that hadn’t heard from the person whose messages used to fill every evening.

For fourteen days he hadn’t written a single thing about her. He hadn’t stopped thinking about her for one of them, and he was beginning to understand that no notebook could make that any easier.
